reader.title: Lynching of Wise in the Turtle Mountains
bases: Settlers who had missed horses overtook Wise, took his rifle and hanged him to a tree, as reported in a Bismarck dispatch (A1, A4, A11).

The dispatch says Wise was hanged by 'several settlers' (A4), 'a body of armed settlers' (A11), with no officer or legal process mentioned, for alleged horse stealing (A1, A4); the account rests on one wire relaying 'private advices' from the settlers' side.

Nearly every report derives from one Bismarck dispatch (A1, A4 and reprints A2, A3, A6-A12); the Maine brief (A5) adds only a different day and place name, and no local or independent account was found.

summary.text: The lynching of Wise was the hanging of a man reported only as Wise by settlers in the Turtle Mountains of Dakota Territory in mid-September 1888, after they accused him of stealing their horses.

The news reached the national press through a single Bismarck dispatch, which papers headlined less for the lynching itself than for the claim that the dead man had once been a prominent citizen of Wyoming.

According to the Bismarck dispatch, Wise had lived in Wyoming Territory, where he had been "prominently mentioned for the legislature," and had come originally from Pennsylvania, where his family was said to live.
Horses had been missed in the vicinity for some time, and the dispatch said it was believed that Wise had taken many of them across the border into Canada.
Citing "private advices from the scene," the dispatch said that several settlers who had missed horses pursued Wise as he was heading toward Manitoba with horses.
They overtook him in a ravine, where he at first "showed fight" but was forced to throw down his rifle and give up the horses.
He was then driven to the nearest tree and hanged.
The day is uncertain: the earliest dispatch, dated Bismarck, September 14, placed the lynching on Wednesday, September 12, while a Maine brief and a New Hampshire summary said Thursday.
The Maine brief also gave the place as "North Mountain" and named no victim.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official inquiry appears in the coverage, and Wise's first name is not given.

In early October a Waynesburg, Pennsylvania, paper reported word that a former congressman named Morgan R. Wise had been lynched "in Arizona or Montana," but it had no particulars and thought the report unfounded; it did not connect that rumor to the Dakota case.
The St. Paul Daily Globe carried the story first, on September 15, under the headline "Hanged to a Tree" and the deck "Summary Punishment Meted Out to a Horse Thief in the Turtle Mountain District."

The same day the Washington Evening Star and the San Antonio Daily Light ran the full dispatch, the Star under "A Once Prominent Citizen of Wyoming Hanged for Horse Stealing" and the Light under "A Gentleman Horse Thief."
The Wichita Eagle followed on September 16 with "A Horse Thief Strung to a Tree," and a Camden, New Jersey, paper redated the wire to September 17 under "A Superior Horse Thief."

Condensed versions then spread through news-in-brief columns in West Virginia, Maine, Minnesota, New Hampshire, Dakota, Rhode Island and Mississippi through the end of September, some placing the event in the "Turtle Creek Mountains" or dating it "on the 14th."
Every version called Wise a horse thief outright rather than an accused one, and none questioned the settlers' account or named any of them.

accounts.label: Bismarck wire (relaying private advices from the scene)
accounts.gist: Settlers who had missed horses overtook Wise in a ravine on his way to Manitoba; he showed fight, gave up his rifle and the horses, and was hanged to the nearest tree on Wednesday.

accounts.label: Maine news brief
accounts.gist: An unnamed horse thief was lynched in Dakota at North Mountain on Thursday.

framing.detail: The St. Paul Daily Globe headlined it 'Hanged to a Tree' with 'Summary Punishment Meted Out to a Horse Thief,' treating the accusation as fact.
Other papers reran the wire under headlines on the victim's past status, such as 'A Gentleman Horse Thief' and 'A Superior Horse Thief.'
News-in-brief columns condensed it to a sentence or two, without comment.

conflicts.note: The earliest dispatch (A1, Bismarck, Sept. 14) says Wednesday and is the best evidence; the ready-print summaries date nearly every item 'on the 14th,' the day the news broke.
The Maine brief's 'North Mountain' is otherwise unattested and matches the wire in every other respect; the wire's Turtle Mountains is the better-supported place.
